explanations: terra: وَتَظَاهَرُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِالْإِثْمِ وَالْعُدْوَانِ describes factions supporting one another in aggression, another conflict use of the back-root as reinforcement.

luna: “Al-qiṣāṣu fī al-qatlā” prescribes retribution in cases of the slain, while allowing pardon and payment. This gives legal shape to the source section's dictionary image of blood whose claim may or may not be pursued. | terra: Retaliation is prescribed for the slain while remission and fair payment remain possible, ensuring that blood receives an acknowledged settlement rather than becoming the unclaimed blood of the dictionary image.

luna: The next ayah after the rule of retribution says “wa-lakum fī al-qiṣāṣi ḥayāh,” that life is preserved through it. It supplies the stated purpose of the blood-claim boundary in 2:178, rather than treating spilled blood as void.
terra: The command is to fight those who fight the believers without transgressing; this establishes the moral boundary governing when martial force may be taken up.
terra: If the opponents cease, Allah's forgiveness and mercy govern the response; with 2:193 it prevents the order to fight from becoming a reason to prolong war after its cause ends.

luna: The parallel command says to fight until fitna ends and, if the other side desists, cease aggression. This repeated boundary clarifies when the source section's end-of-war laying down of arms can occur. | terra: Fighting is ordered until persecution ends, and if the opponents cease, hostility ceases except against wrongdoers; it names an endpoint at which war's burdens no longer remain in use.

luna: This command tells believers to stand devoutly before God in prayer. It is a precise devotional counterpart to the source section's standing after finishing work and its immediate direction toward the Lord. | terra: وَقُومُوا لِلَّهِ قَانِتِينَ explicitly commands standing for Allah, giving the section's post-struggle upright stance its stated direction; the next ayah carries that prayer into danger.
terra: Prayer continues on foot or mounted under fear, then remembrance follows when safety returns; with 2:238 it stages worship through danger and after danger has passed.

terra: The faithful minority says many a small force has overcome a large one by Allah's permission; it supplies the overcoming sense developed in the section and leads directly to the prayer of 2:250.

luna: At the battle with Jalut, the fighters ask “afriġ ʿalaynā ṣabran” and for firm feet and help. The source section's root note gives pouring as a sense of f-r-ġ; here what is poured into the combatants is patience. | terra: Facing Goliath's host, the fighters pray أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًا, ask that their feet be made firm, and seek victory; it is the section's battlefield use of pouring from the FRG root.

luna: The next ayah says “fa-hazamūhum bi-idhn Allāh”: Jalut's force is defeated and David kills Jalut. It supplies the battle's outcome after 2:250's plea for help and illuminates the source section's dictionary sense of w-z-r as overcoming. | terra: They defeat Goliath's force by Allah's permission and David kills Goliath, completing the battle whose fighters asked for poured patience in 2:250.
terra: The prayer asks that no crushing load be imposed, seeks pardon, and ends وَانصُرْنَا عَلَى الْقَوْمِ الْكَافِرِينَ; burden relief and victory over an enemy meet in a single appeal to the Lord.

luna: God says He will make Jesus' followers prevail over those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. This is another specific formulation of the source section's dictionary sense of ẓ-h-r as religious dominance, with a different prophetic community and a stated duration.
terra: The Messenger leaves early to station believers in their positions for battle, a concrete deployment scene at the opposite temporal edge from dismissing the war formation and its gear.
terra: Allah reminds the believers that He gave them victory at Badr while they were weak, making divine help answer the inadequacy of the fighting force.
terra: The Prophet reassures the believers that their Lord can reinforce them with three thousand angels, specifying the aid recalled in 3:123 and interpreted in 3:126.
terra: Patience and reverence under an immediate enemy assault are answered with further angelic reinforcement; the ayah states the fighters' stance while help approaches.

terra: After the promised reinforcements of 3:124-125, the ayah says they are reassurance and that victory comes only from Allah; it distinguishes the true source of prevalence from its visible means.

luna: After the battle at Uhud, this ayah tells believers not to lose heart or grieve and promises they will be uppermost if they remain believers. It gives a battle-context formulation of prevailing after a setback, alongside the source section's victory sense.

luna: This ayah says that if a wound has touched the believers, a similar wound has touched the opposing people, and that God rotates such days among people. It concretely connects to the source section's dictionary image of a blow that spills blood, while showing battle wounds and fortunes as reciprocal and changing. | terra: The ayah compares the wound that struck the believers with a wound that struck their opponents, making the section's bleeding blow part of the alternating fortunes of battle.
terra: Prophetic fighters do not weaken, flag, or surrender after what strikes them; this steadfast conduct supplies the human stance that becomes explicit prayer in 3:147.
terra: Believers fighting with prophets pray for forgiveness, firm feet, and victory over disbelievers; like 2:250, battle directs their stance and speech to their Lord.

terra: If Allah grants victory no one can overcome the believers, and if He forsakes them no other helper can prevail; the ayah locates battlefield superiority in divine aid rather than equipment alone.
terra: Those who answer Allah and the Messenger after the wound has struck them remain active after battle injury, continuing the wound scene developed in 3:140 rather than treating it as the end.
terra: Believers remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides, repeating outside battle the full-posture remembrance that follows the fear prayer in 4:103.
terra: Believers are commanded to be patient, outlast opposition, remain watchfully stationed, and fear Allah; the martial posture is held together by a Godward stance.
terra: Allah's wish to lighten people's load is immediately grounded in human weakness, closely repeating the logic of 8:66's battlefield lightening because weakness is known.
terra: خُذُوا حِذْرَكُمْ and the command to mobilize in groups or all together show equipment and readiness being taken up, clarifying what the postwar laying-down reverses.

terra: Some believers were first told to restrain their hands and establish prayer, then recoiled when fighting was prescribed; this reverses the section's movement from completed fighting into prayer.
terra: Those who withdraw, do not fight, and offer peace may not be attacked; restrained hands become a concrete sign that the war relation has ended.
terra: Unlike the withdrawing group in 4:90, people who neither withdraw nor restrain their hands remain combatants; the pair defines the conduct that does or does not allow weapons to fall.

luna: The source section's dictionary form for f-r-ġ describes blood that goes unclaimed; 4:92 requires blood-money to be delivered to the slain person's family for accidental killing, unless they waive it. The verse gives a concrete legal opposite to blood left without claim. | terra: Accidental killing requires freeing a believer and paying compensation to the victim's family unless they remit it; this supplies a concrete Quranic procedure by which shed blood does not pass without account.
terra: On campaign, believers must verify rather than deny the faith of one who offers peace; an offered peaceful relation interrupts the assumption that the person remains an armed enemy.
terra: The comparison between those sitting and those striving explicitly excepts people with disabling harm, setting a bodily limit on the burden of fighting.

luna: This ayah permits shortening prayer while traveling if attack by disbelievers is feared. It establishes the danger around the next verse's armed prayer, where setting weapons down is only a temporary allowance. | terra: The permission to shorten prayer when an enemy attack is feared introduces the danger managed in 4:102; its own contribution is to keep prayer possible while the force is still armed and exposed.

luna: The source section cites “an taḍaʿū aslihatakum”: during the fear-prayer, rain or illness can permit setting arms aside while precautions remain. Here the weapon is put down temporarily within active danger, unlike the section's imagined end of war. | terra: The fear-prayer command permits أَن تَضَعُوا أَسْلِحَتَكُمْ because of rain or illness while worshippers take turns standing; it directly stages the section's weapon-laying and prayer stance.

luna: After the fear-prayer, this ayah tells believers to remember God standing, sitting, or lying down, and to pray normally when safe. It continues 4:102's armed prayer and makes the transition from combat vigilance to devotion explicit. | terra: After the fear prayer of 4:102, believers remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying down and establish regular prayer once secure; this ayah supplies the calm stance after weapons may be lowered.

luna: The ayah says not to weaken in pursuing the enemy, since they suffer too and believers hope in God. In the same war-prayer passage, it marks the active struggle that must continue before the source section's arms can be laid down at war's end. | terra: Believers must not weaken in pursuing the enemy: both sides suffer pain, but believers hope from Allah what the enemy does not; the burden of continued fighting is sustained by a Godward hope.
terra: A hostile people intend to stretch out their hands against the believers, but Allah restrains those hands; the prevented attack is another way a threatened fight is disarmed.

luna: This ayah gives the Torah rule “al-nafsa bi-al-nafs” and permits relinquishing the claim as charity. It is another specific legal account of a slain person's blood being pursued or waived, matching the source section's f-r-ġ dictionary sense. | terra: وَالْجُرُوحَ قِصَاصٌ makes wounds subject to requital, directly illuminating the dictionary image of an open, bleeding wound and blood that must not be left without claim.
terra: كُلَّمَا أَوْقَدُوا نَارًا لِلْحَرْبِ أَطْفَأَهَا اللَّهُ depicts God extinguishing war whenever it is kindled, a nonlexical counterpart to war laying down its own burdens.
terra: Game within reach of hands and spears names the spear outside warfare; it shows one implement in the section's war kit retaining a controlled use when battle is absent.

luna: The source section's dictionary note treats wizr as war gear borne on a back; 6:31 says the deniers carry their “awzārahum ʿalā ẓuhūrihim.” The same burden-and-back image is reversed: their loads remain on them at judgment rather than being removed. | terra: يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ joins both of the section's concrete elements: burdens are carried on backs, though here the load is moral and remains disastrous rather than removable armor.
terra: دَمًا مَسْفُوحًا names blood poured or flowing out, a concrete counterpart to the blood flowing from the wide wound in the section's FRG dictionary note, though here the context is food law.
terra: لَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى makes each soul's moral burden nontransferable, in contrast with physical war gear that another hand can remove.

luna: After Pharaoh threatens the newly believing magicians with mutilation and crucifixion, they ask “afriġ ʿalaynā ṣabran.” The same root-formula as 2:250 pours patience over people facing lethal violence, extending the source section's struggle image beyond battlefield combat. | terra: The threatened magicians repeat أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًا as they face mutilation and death, showing the section's pouring of patience as a stance toward God under violent pressure.
terra: وَيَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَالْأَغْلَالَ uses the same construction of placing a load away from people; the release from burden and bonds clarifies the bodily relief heard in 94:2.
terra: The fighters call to their Lord for help and receive the promise of angelic reinforcement; battle pressure is answered by God rather than borne through equipment alone.
terra: The reinforcement promised in 8:9 is reassurance for the fighters' hearts, while victory is said to come only from Allah; this fixes the source of the overcoming imagined by the section.

luna: At Badr, God sends rain to purify the believers, strengthen their hearts, and make their feet firm. This parallels the battle prayer in 2:250 for patience and firm footing, showing divine support that lets fighters stand under pressure. | terra: In the same battle sequence, rain purifies the believers and God binds their hearts and firms their feet; rain, battlefield vulnerability, divine relief, and an upright stance meet here.

terra: The command to strike above necks and fingertips stages the use of cutting weapons on the battlefield, giving the section's otherwise named sword a Quranic action even though the implement itself is not named.
terra: Believers meeting an advancing army are forbidden to turn their backs; during combat the armored back must hold its line, whereas the section removes its load only after struggle.
terra: The fighters' killing and the Messenger's casting are attributed ultimately to Allah, locating battlefield efficacy beyond the warrior and his visible implements.

luna: This ayah commands fighting until persecution ends and religion belongs wholly to God, then says to stop if the other side desists. It gives a specific condition for the cessation that the source section pictures as war laying down its burdens.
terra: When believers meet an enemy force, they are told both to stand firm and remember Allah much; their posture is against the army while its inward direction remains toward the Lord.
terra: Continuing the battlefield command of 8:45, believers must obey, avoid disputes that dissolve courage and strength, and remain patient; it explains how their firm stance is maintained.
terra: Satan first claims that no one can overcome the force, then turns on his heels when the armies appear; false confidence in superiority collapses into retreat.

luna: Believers are told to prepare whatever strength they can, including warhorses, to deter an enemy. This is the arming phase opposite to the source section's scene of putting battle gear down once war is over. | terra: Preparing every available force and tethered horse is the deliberate arming that precedes conflict, the temporal opposite of letting war's equipment fall when it is over.

luna: “If they incline to peace, incline to it” sets a clear boundary for armed conflict. The source section pictures the moment war drops its gear; this ayah describes the decision to turn from fighting toward peace. | terra: If the enemy inclines to peace, the Messenger must incline to it and trust Allah; this gives a relational criterion for moving from armed struggle to peace.

luna: This ayah commands the Prophet to urge the believers to fight and states the initial one-to-ten endurance ratio. The next ayah, 8:66, lightens that military burden; this verse supplies the demand that is eased. | terra: Patient believers are initially charged with overcoming a much larger force; this is the combat weight that 8:66 immediately says Allah has lightened.

luna: The source section explicitly cites “al-āna khaffafa Allāhu ʿankum,” God's easing of the military demand after the prior verse's ten-to-one ratio. This is a direct wartime counterpart to the load removed from a fighter. | terra: Allah says He has now lightened the believers' combat obligation because He knows their weakness; this is the section's load being reduced in the middle of its actual war setting.
terra: A prophet may not take captives before thoroughly subduing the enemy in the land; beside 47:4, it marks a boundary before the battle can be treated as complete.
terra: إِنْ يَظْهَرُوا عَلَيْكُمْ means the treaty-breakers' gaining mastery over believers, using ZHR for the hostile dominance that the section's promise of true religious prevalence opposes.

terra: Believers are told to fight while Allah punishes and disgraces the enemy through their hands, grants victory, and heals believing hearts; combat, divine aid, and its relieving outcome are held together.

luna: The source section's root note says ẓ-h-r can mean prevailing; 9:33 uses “li-yuẓhirahu ʿalā al-dīni kullihi,” to make the religion prevail over all religion. This is the specific Qur'anic use of victory named in the section. | terra: لِيُظْهِرَهُ عَلَى الدِّينِ كُلِّهِ is the cited ZHR sense of making the Messenger's religion prevail, turning the back-root into superiority rather than a burdened body part.

luna: When called to fight, some “iththāqaltum ilā al-arḍ,” grow heavy and cling to the earth; the passage contrasts this with seeking the nearer life. It reverses the source section's fighter who bears gear through battle and lays it down only after the conflict. | terra: When called to mobilize, some become heavy and cling to the earth; this earthbound heaviness reverses the section's relieved addressee who rises after his load is removed.

luna: The mobilization command says “infirū khifāfan wa-thiqālan.” The phrase can mean light and heavy in more than one way, but in its war setting it suggests going out under differing loads, the opposite phase from the source section's gear being laid down. | terra: انْفِرُوا خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا orders believers to go forth light or heavy, making the fighter's weight and mobility explicit before the later image of the load being removed.
terra: During the campaign, the hypocrites overturn plans until truth comes and وَظَهَرَ أَمْرُ اللَّهِ; ZHR gives Allah's cause the prevailing position despite hostile obstruction.
terra: The weak, sick, and unequipped incur no blame for not joining battle if sincere to Allah and His Messenger, directly paralleling the section's battlefield concessions and lightened load.
terra: Those who sincerely seek transport for the campaign but cannot be equipped turn away in tears; the ayah makes lack of martial means a concrete reason the battle load cannot be assumed.
terra: The covenant of believers who fight, kill, and are killed puts the full mortal cost of battle immediately before the worshipping portrait in 9:112.
terra: The ayah beside the fighting covenant of 9:111 portrays the believers as repentant worshippers who praise, bow, and prostrate, bringing combat commitment and Godward posture into one passage.
terra: No thirst, hunger, or نَصَب afflicts the believers on campaign without being credited, placing the NSP root's toil sense inside actual movement against an enemy.
terra: Paradise is a place where no نَصَب touches its people and they are never expelled; its permanent freedom from fatigue contrasts with the commanded exertion of فَانصَبْ after one task ends.

luna: This ayah says that those who mislead will carry their own burdens fully and some burdens of those they misled on the Day of Resurrection. The source section's dictionary note uses wizr for war gear carried and laid down; this same root becomes a moral load that accumulates instead of being removed. | terra: Misleaders carry their own أَوْزَار in full and portions of the burdens of those they mislead, showing how the war-equipment plural also names accumulated moral liabilities.

luna: Among God's protections are “sarābīla taqīkum ba'sakum,” garments that guard you in battle. This names the same protective clothing function as the source section's armor, which is carried through conflict and set down when it ends. | terra: وَسَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُم بَأْسَكُمْ names garments that protect people from one another's violence, supplying the Quranic counterpart to the section's armor worn in battle.
terra: The repeated rule that no burden-bearer bears another's burden preserves personal accountability against a purely physical reading of the load removed in the section.

luna: The source section's dictionary note glosses f-r-ġ in “zehebe damuhu farghan” as blood going unclaimed. For an unjustly slain person, 17:33 grants the heir authority but forbids excess in killing, setting a limit on whether blood is left without redress. | terra: The heir of one killed unjustly receives authority to seek redress while being forbidden excess; this is the Quranic opposite of the section's dictionary phrase for blood that goes vain because no claim is made.

terra: The sleepers fear that if their people يَظْهَرُوا عَلَيْكُمْ they will stone them or force them back into their creed; ZHR here is persecutors' mastery, the adverse face of the section's victory sense.
terra: The ruler asks the people to assist with strength so he can make a protective barrier; this collective defensive labor leads into the iron and poured copper of 18:96.

terra: أُفْرِغْ عَلَيْهِ قِطْرًا uses FRG for literally pouring molten copper over an iron barrier; the protective metalwork meets both the section's armor and its metaphor of patience poured over fighters.
terra: Moses asks for a وَزِير from his family; within the following sequence, the WZR-root person is one who helps with a task rather than the burden itself.
terra: Moses asks that his strength or support be tightened through Aaron, making the helper requested in 20:29 an answer to bodily and vocational strain.
terra: وَأَشْرِكْهُ فِي أَمْرِي states that Aaron is to share Moses' task, the practical way a helper lightens what one person would otherwise bear alone.
terra: The purpose of that shared task is كَيْ نُسَبِّحَكَ كَثِيرًا, so relief through a helper leads into abundant glorification just as the section's released fighter turns toward his Lord.
terra: Moses adds that the brothers may remember God much, completing the helper-and-shared-work sequence with the Godward attention it enables.

terra: Whoever turns from the Reminder يَحْمِلُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وِزْرًا; the singular word is again a load actually carried, but its setting makes it enduring moral consequence rather than removable arms.
terra: The burden of 20:100 is called a terrible حِمْل on the resurrection day; this continuation makes explicit the weight already carried in the preceding ayah.

luna: God teaches David to make coats of armor “lituhṣinakum min ba'sikum,” to protect you from your violence. The armor worn and later laid down in the source section has this explicit defensive purpose. | terra: David is taught صَنْعَةَ لَبُوسٍ لَكُمْ so armor may protect people from their violence; the protective coat is one of the very implements imagined in the laid-down war kit.
terra: Permission to fight is granted to those being wronged; it begins the sequence whose endpoint in 22:41 is established prayer after the threatened worshipping community is given footing.
terra: The expulsion of believers and defense of monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques make protection of worship the purpose of the struggle begun in 22:39 and resolved in 22:41.
terra: Those established after the conflict of 22:39-40 establish prayer and give alms; this is a direct Quranic sequence from fighting and victory to standing in service of God.
terra: The command to strive for Allah says He placed no constriction in religion and then orders prayer; exertion, an unburdened religion, and worship form the section's sequence.
terra: حِينَ تَضَعُونَ ثِيَابَكُمْ مِنَ الظَّهِيرَةِ uses W-D-A for laying aside worn clothing at the hour of rest, a domestic analogue to removing the warrior's worn covering after exertion.

terra: Older women are permitted أَن يَضَعْنَ ثِيَابَهُنَّ under stated limits; the same physical verb for putting off a covering clarifies the section's bodily image without making the clothing martial.
terra: Allah gives Moses the Book and appoints Aaron with him as a وَزِير, repeating the WZR-root image of a companion supplied for a demanding commission.

luna: The source section's root note connects ẓ-h-r with the back and prevailing; here the unbeliever is “ʿalā rabbihi ẓahīran,” a supporter against his Lord. That reversed direction sharpens the source section's insistence that the renewed stance is toward the Lord.
terra: The servants of the Merciful spend the night لِرَبِّهِمْ prostrating and standing, explicitly assigning the standing posture to their Lord.
terra: God is the one who sees the Messenger when he rises, placing the prophetic act of standing under direct divine regard.
terra: The Messenger's movement among those prostrating completes 26:218's rising as a worship scene rather than a stance of hostility.
terra: Moses' mother's heart becomes فَارِغًا under fear and nearly exposes him; this emptying under pressure contrasts with fighters asking that patience be poured into them from the same FRG root.

terra: After completing the work of watering the two women's flock, Moses withdraws and addresses his need to his Lord; this is a specific nonbattle parallel to finishing exertion and turning Godward.

luna: The verse says that the misleaders will carry their own burdens and additional burdens with them. The source section's dictionary root wizr evokes gear borne in battle and then set aside; here the burden in its moral sense is added and carried forward. | terra: The wrongdoers carry their own heavy loads and additional loads with them; although it uses the weight vocabulary rather than وزر, it preserves the section's picture of burdens borne by a person.

luna: “Those who strive in Us” are promised guidance to God's ways. This states the direction implicit in the source section's fanṣab followed by “wa-ilā rabbika”: effort is reoriented toward God, and that effort leads to His ways.
terra: The Romans' defeat states one side of military overcoming; 30:3 immediately promises that this status will be reversed rather than remain fixed.
terra: After their defeat, the Romans will overcome in a few years, showing victory and defeat exchanging places as the section's paired senses of struggle and prevalence allow.

terra: Allah turns the confederates back without their gain and كَفَى اللَّهُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الْقِتَالَ; the believers are released from fighting itself, the condition under which the section's gear can come off.
terra: The People of the Book who ظَاهَرُوهُمْ had backed the confederates are brought down from their fortresses; the root depicts martial support ending in defeat rather than prevalence.

luna: God softens iron for David; the next ayah, 34:11, specifies that it becomes coats of mail. The metal-working scene supplies the material step behind the armor named in the source section. | terra: Allah makes iron pliable for David immediately before the command to fashion coats of mail in 34:11; this ayah supplies the transformation of the armor's heavy material.

luna: David is told to make full coats of mail and measure the links. That is a concrete instance of the armor in the source section's image, down to the linked construction of battle gear. | terra: David is told to make full coats of mail and measure their links, an unusually exact Quranic view of the armor whose weight the section imagines removed after combat.

terra: A heavily laden soul may call for help with its load, yet none of it can be carried even by a relative; this sharply bounds the armor image, since moral burden cannot simply be taken onto another back.
terra: The people of the lasting abode praise God because neither نَصَب nor weariness touches them, presenting final rest beyond the section's recurring rhythm of relief followed by fresh labor.

luna: The passage says that God's party will prevail. This is a further nonlexical formulation of the section's dictionary note that ẓ-h-r can mean prevailing, here cast as the outcome of the messengers' conflict with their deniers.
terra: In a warning about disbelief and gratitude, لَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى again marks moral وزر as an inalienable responsibility rather than discarded equipment.
terra: Pharaoh describes his people as ظَاهِرِينَ in the land, using ZHR for political ascendancy; the doomed boast tests the moral value of mere upper-handedness.
terra: Repelling evil with what is better can turn a hostile person into a devoted friend, reversing the section's dictionary scene of enmity being raised and maintained against someone.

luna: The source section's root note identifies ẓahr as the back bearing a burden; 43:13 uses “ʿalā ẓuhūrihi” for the backs of riding animals, then tells riders to remember God's favor. The shared load-bearing body part is clear, though the contrast between strain and transport is interpretive.

luna: The source section's dictionary note calls evzār the weapons of war; 47:4 says “ḥattā taḍaʿa al-ḥarbu awzārahā,” until war itself lays them down. The shift from war's gear to the addressee's removed burden makes the release audible as war's ending. | terra: The battle command uses the section's exact verb and plural noun, حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ الْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا: war itself lays down its equipment, making the removed load in 94:2 sound like armor taken off when fighting ends.
terra: Believers who support Allah are promised His support and firm feet, joining divine victory with the upright firmness sought by the fighters in 2:250.
terra: Believers are forbidden to weaken and call for peace while they have the upper hand; it marks the danger of treating war as finished and laying down its burden prematurely.
terra: The blind, lame, and sick are explicitly exempted from blame in the mobilization context, another concrete limit on who must bear the work of battle.
terra: Alongside promised spoils, Allah restrains people's hands from the believers; successful combat thus includes a divinely imposed cessation of attack.

luna: After the conquest at Mecca, God says He restrained both sides' hands from each other. The image of hands held back gives a concrete boundary to the armed scene in which the source section imagines weapons finally being set down. | terra: After granting victory, Allah restrains the enemy's hands from the believers and theirs from the enemy, staging the mutual cessation of violence behind the laid-down war kit.

luna: The source section's dictionary note links ẓ-h-r with prevailing; after the treaty and the promise of clear victory, this ayah repeats “li-yuẓhirahu ʿalā al-dīni kullihi.” It places that prevailing purpose in the context of the Messenger's mission. | terra: This ayah repeats لِيُظْهِرَهُ عَلَى الدِّينِ كُلِّهِ, confirming that the section's victory sense of ZHR is a recurring description of the Messenger's mission.
terra: The same companions are firm against the disbelievers yet seen bowing and prostrating as they seek God's favor, placing combat stance and worship stance in one portrait.
terra: Believers fight the aggressing party only until it returns to Allah's command, then must reconcile justly; the ayah defines when communal fighting is to stop.
terra: After 49:9 ends armed conflict and orders justice, this ayah grounds reconciliation in the believers' brotherhood; it states the relation that should replace fighting.

luna: Addressed to the Prophet, this ayah commands patience for the Lord's judgment and glorification of the Lord when he rises. It closely joins the source section's two steps: stand after the task, then direct the stance to God. | terra: The Messenger is told to endure for his Lord's judgment and وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ حِينَ تَقُومُ; rising is explicitly turned into praise of the Lord.
terra: The maxim in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham that no bearer bears another's burden gives the same ancient boundary to the section's armor metaphor.
terra: The enemy host is promised defeat and will turn its back, giving a compact battlefield realization of overcoming and the end of its confident martial stance.

luna: The source section's root note connects faraghta with becoming free of a task; here God says “sanafruġu lakum,” addressing humans and jinn before the challenge in 55:33. The speaker and direction reverse: human devotion after work becomes God's announced attention to his audience.
terra: Those who spent and fought before the conquest are distinguished from those who did so afterward, making victory a real threshold that changes the weight and risk of martial service.
terra: Iron is said to contain mighty force and benefits for people; alongside the armor passages, it identifies the material power stored in the equipment that can be carried or laid down.
terra: The hypocrites take their oaths as a جُنَّة, a shield, transferring one object from the section's war kit into a moral image of self-protection used to obstruct God's path.
terra: The expelled people believe their fortresses will protect them, but the defenses fail when God's judgment comes; communal armor proves unable to provide the security expected of it.

terra: Abraham's people say enmity and hatred have become openly established between the two sides; this is a concrete nonlexical instance of hostility being set toward someone, unlike فَانصَبْ directed toward the Lord.
terra: Those who neither fight believers for religion nor expel them remain proper objects of kindness and justice; paired with 60:9, noncombatant conduct sets the boundary of the hostile relation.
terra: The ayah distinguishes those who fought and expelled believers and ظَاهَرُوا عَلَىٰ إِخْرَاجِكُمْ, using the back-root for active support of hostile force.

luna: This ayah praises believers who fight in God's cause in aligned ranks, like a joined structure. It shows the organized battle-facing stance that the source section distinguishes from its post-task stance directed toward the Lord. | terra: Allah loves those who fight in a row like a solid structure, presenting the armed team as a disciplined, mutually supporting formation before its implements are laid down.

luna: This ayah repeats the source section's root example, “li-yuẓhirahu ʿalā al-dīni kullihi,” and says the purpose stands despite the polytheists' dislike. It makes explicit the resistance against which the religion's prevailing is measured. | terra: The third occurrence of لِيُظْهِرَهُ عَلَى الدِّينِ كُلِّهِ completes the Quranic refrain behind the section's move from a back carrying armor to religion being made uppermost.
terra: Believers are called to strive with wealth and lives; this states the costly struggle whose promised outcome in 61:13 is divine help and a near victory.
terra: نَصْرٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَفَتْحٌ قَرِيبٌ promises divine help and near victory after the striving of 61:11, supplying the victorious completion of the struggle.
terra: Allah strengthens the believers against their enemy and they become ظَاهِرِينَ; this is the ZHR root in the section's precise sense of prevailing in a conflict.
terra: When Friday prayer is finished, believers disperse to seek God's bounty; its worship-then-work sequence reverses 94:7-8's finish-work-then-direct-yourself-to-God sequence.
terra: This ayah repeats the image of oaths taken as a جُنَّة, confirming the shield's Quranic metaphorical use as cover for hostile obstruction.

luna: The verse promises that God will bring ease after hardship. This matches the specific sequence the source section develops: the war's weight is borne through struggle, then the burden is set down as the conflict ends.
terra: People rush toward a نُصُب as though to an erected goal; the shared root and directed movement form a contrary orientation to rising and directing desire toward the Lord.

luna: The command “qumi al-layla” tells the wrapped Prophet to stand in prayer at night. It offers a concrete devotional form of the source section's fanṣab, whose stance is directed by the following “wa-ilā rabbika.” | terra: قُمِ اللَّيْلَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا is another direct command to the Messenger to rise for worship, clarifying the devotional posture heard in فَانصَبْ.

luna: God says “qawlan thaqīlā,” a weighty word will be cast upon the Prophet. The image of revelation as a weight borne by the same prophetic addressee gives a non-weapon parallel to the source section's burden on the back.

luna: The Prophet is told that he has a long occupation by day; 73:8 then directs him to remember and devote himself to his Lord. Together they make explicit a rhythm of completing worldly work and turning to devotion, as in the source section's reading of faraghta then fanṣab. | terra: The Messenger has prolonged occupation during the day; this supplies the unfinished worldly exertion before the directed remembrance in 73:8.

luna: The same prophetic address commands “wa-udhkur isma rabbika wa-tabattal ilayhi tabtīlā,” remembering the Lord and devoting oneself wholly to Him. This gives a close parallel to the source section's direction after the task: turn the renewed effort toward the Lord. | terra: وَاذْكُرِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ directs the Messenger wholly toward his Lord after the daytime occupation named in 73:7.

terra: The eased night-recitation command expressly accounts for the sick and for others fighting in Allah's way, then commands prayer; it joins illness, combat, lightened duty, and worship as the section does.

luna: “Qum fa-andhir” commands the Prophet to rise and warn. This is a specific prophetic command to stand into further work, paralleling the source section's interpretation of fanṣab after one task is finished.

luna: After commands to rise, warn, and purify, this ayah says “wa-li-rabbika faṣbir,” for your Lord be patient. Its explicit direction to the Lord parallels the source section's final turn away from an opponent and toward God.
terra: Human beings are described as laboring toward their Lord until meeting Him; the destination makes exertion Godward in the same relation expressed by فَانصَبْ followed by وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
terra: عَامِلَةٌ نَاصِبَةٌ depicts laboring exhaustion that leads into punishment, a dark reversal of the purposeful effort toward the Lord commanded by فَانصَبْ.

luna: After recalling the abundance given to the Prophet, this ayah commands him to pray and sacrifice for his Lord. It offers a concrete act of renewed service directed to God, paralleling the source section's movement from completed labor to turning toward the Lord.
terra: The arrival of Allah's help and victory supplies the completed struggle that leads to the worship command in 110:3.
terra: People entering Allah's religion in crowds states what the victory of 110:1 has accomplished before the Messenger is redirected to praise in 110:3.
terra: فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ follows victory with a command to glorify and seek forgiveness, closely matching the section's turn from a finished struggle toward the Lord.
